"Sound levels of all playbacks were normalized to 90% of
the maximum pressure levels, and playback volumes at each nest

exposure_span_notes: Construction-noise playback occurred on 1–4 treatment days; when more than one day was used, playback days were separated by two silent days.
exposure_notes: "We utilized a gradient of chronic traffic noise (from approximately < 60 to > 75 dBA) and experimentally added intermittent noise disturbances to nest boxes where females were incubating completed clutches of eggs in a combined comparative-experimental design."... "the total length of each playback file was 10 hours. randomization_notes: "Active nests in boxes placed near and far from large roads were randomly assigned as treatments or controls for experimental playbacks during incubation."

outcome_notes: they measured outcomes from "10 AM and 6 PM". control_sound_characteristics: "the control (65 dBA ±0.82; W =45.00, n=9, P=0.004), although this difference might vary as ambient sound pressure levels typically change over the course of a day... 62.4–68.7 dBA over the noon hour (current study)."

"The study found no significant difference between the experimental (high noise) and control (ambient noise) groups for any of the measured outcomes, despite a 20 dBA difference in noise exposure.
It may be the unpredictability of traffic noise that causes stress in nestlings rather than the actual traffic sounds. Nest- lings in our control group experienced not only ambient urban noise that followed typical daily patterns, but also spontaneous, unpredictable sounds such as sirens, garbage trucks and barking dogs, which may serve as stressors. title: Do Black Ducks and Wood Ducks Habituate to Aircraft Disturbance?
sp_context_notes: “We conducted field experiments with captive, wild strain black ducks hatched in spring 1991 at a North Carolina State University (NCSU) experimental farm unit in Raleigh.” “The wood ducks were hatched in 1991 from eggs collected from nests of wild-strain birds in North Carolina.”
bird_sex_notes: The study included both males and females. In the field experiment, black ducks at Piney Island were 11 M, 9 F, and the NCSU comparison group was 8 M, 10 F. In the simulated-noise experiment, black-duck groups were 2 M, 2 F, and wood-duck groups were described as mixed sexes.
experiment_context_notes: Experiment 1: Captive American black ducks were housed in a 12 x 12 x 2.5-m aviary located on a military aircraft target range. Experiment 2: Captive American black ducks and wood ducks were studied in a 9.7 x 29.3-m pen constructed on an experimental farm unit pond
noise_type_notes: They simulated military and commercial aircraft noise: “we subjected captive, wild-strain American black ducks (Anas rubripes) and wood ducks (Aix sponsa) to actual and simulated activities of jet aircraft.” The field experiment took place near “Piney Island, a military aircraft target range,” and the simulated-noise experiment used “6 different recordings of jet noise.”
noise_characteristics: Playbacks: “We used tape recordings of 6 different aircraft overflights to simulate actual overflights (Table 2). “The rate at which the noise increased (onset rate) and decreased (offset rate) varied between recordings, but noise amplitudes were standardized to 84.8 dBA (Leq = 63.2).”
exposure_span_notes: The Playback experiment: reported a range from 2, ducks were generally exposed to simulated aircraft noise for 4 days, but the last two black-duck replicate groups were exposed for only 2 days.
exposure_notes: Authors do not explicitly call the birds juveniles/immatures, but hatch year and winter exposure indicate juvenile/pre-breeding birds.
experimental_procedures_notes: simulated overflights between 0800 and 1400 each day
randomization_notes: The only explicit randomization is that the 36 overflights were played at random intervals, which refers to playback timing, not treatment allocation.
control_sound_characteristics: NR
control_sound_notes: "Within-subject pre-exposure baseline: birds were placed in the same outdoor NCSU farm-pond pen, allowed to adjust to the surroundings for 1 day, and then observed for 2 days before simulated aircraft-noise disturbance began. No separate concurrent behavioural control group was used during the playback exposure phase. For the black-duck body-mass comparison, before beginning the experiment, two additional groups of four black ducks each were placed in pens and fed whole-kernel corn in the same manner as the experimental birds; these groups were not exposed to simulated overflights and served as controls for mass change.”
outcome_notes: Playback experiment measured behavioural habituation/time-activity budgets in response to simulated aircraft-noise playbacks, including aircraft-induced alert and swimming responses. It also measured black-duck body mass change before and after the simulated-noise experiment, used as a body-condition/energetic outcome.
general_comment: For the playback experient: the authors concluded that simulated aircraft noise caused initial behavioural disturbance in both duck species, but the response pattern differed by species. Black ducks showed habituation: their aircraft-induced behaviours decreased from about 25% on the first exposure day to about 8% by day 4. Wood ducks did not show a consistent decline across groups, suggesting that habituation to aircraft noise may be species-specific. They also found no clear evidence that simulated noise caused additional body-mass loss, because mass loss did not differ between noise-exposed black ducks and non-noise controls.

general_comment: "We found a delay in female response latencies to male song in the noisy condition compared to the control condition on the first day of noise exposure. Males from the noise treatment group, not directly exposed to noise themselves, sang closer to the nest box within 3 days after the start of exposure. 4. The male’s closer proximity to the nest box most likely led to the observed higher song amplitudes at the noisy nest boxes compared to quiet control nest boxes, and explains why the inside signal-to-noise ratios were restored to equal levels between treatment and control nest boxes after several days of exposure. 5. The initial difference between treatment groups in female response latencies at the start of exposure also disappeared accordingly. 6. Our results strongly suggest an active role for female birds in steering male song behaviour under noisy conditions. Males did not receive direct exposure during intra-pair communication, but adjusted their behaviour in the predicted direction. These data are important to understand the mechanisms related to communication in noise and reveal the critical role of ecology in shaping animal interactions."

control_sound_notes: Control nests were exposed only to baseline ambient (natural) traffic noise. Experimental nests were on average 23 dBA louder than controls; based on the reported 80–90 dBA experimental range, the inferred control level is approximately 57–67 dBA (midpoint ≈ 62 dBA). Frequency NR. “Control nest boxes were also equipped with headphones and an MP3 player but were exposed only to baseline ambient (natural) traffic noise.”
outcome_notes: parental provisioning and nestling condition, offspring provisioning and fledging success, begging call
general_comment: "We found that the minimum frequency of the begging calls was higher in nestlings within experimental broods (exposed to traffic-noise playback) compared to that of nestlings in the control broods (exposed only to ambient noise). Also, nestlings in experimental broods continued to beg at a higher minimum frequency but with a narrowed bandwidth after the playback was stopped. Parental provisioning rates did not differ between control and experimental broods, nor did fledging success, although nestlings in the experimental group were in poorer condition. Our findings suggest that urban thrivers are affected by increasing traffic noise but have the phenotypic flexibility to adapt at a young age to maintain critical parent-offspring communication."
